newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran paper says less "U.S. hostility" possible.
newsitem.headline: Iran paper says less "U.S. hostility" possible.

text.p: An influential Iranian newspaper said on Sunday the United States might soften its anti-Iran policies if President Bill Clinton is re-elected in November.

The daily Iran News, which often reflects the views of Iran's foreign ministry, said an administration reshuffle by Clinton during a second term "could pave the way for reduced hostility in U.S. foreign policy (towards Iran)".

The newspaper was commenting on remarks by Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau who said on Thursday he was hopeful the United States would begin dialogue with Iran within the next four years if Clinton is re-elected in November.
Iran News on Saturday quoted Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Mahmoud Vaezi as saying: "Pelletreau's statement does not tally with U.S. actions."

"If Washington learns and understands the realities and the true nature of Iran's Islamic revolution and decides to deal with Iran on the basis of mutual and equal respect, then and only then we can say that America's words and deeds are one and the same," Vaezi added.
The United States broke diplomatic ties with Iran in 1980 over the seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran by Moslem militants who held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.
The hardline conservative daily Jomhuri Eslami on Sunday blasted Pelletreau's remarks as an "election publicity ploy used by Clinton...for 'domestic consumption'".

"This is not the first time that Washington officials have requested dialogue with Tehran and, naturally, they will not get a positive answer this time either," the newspaper quoted an unnamed informed official as saying.

The United States imposed a trade and investment ban on Iran in June 1995, accusing it of sponsoring terrorism and seeking to develop nuclear weapons. Iran denies the charges and says the United States is bent on destroying the Islamic government.
A U.S. law in effect since August tightened the sanctions to include foreign firms.
Iranian officials say their country has no favourite in the U.S. presidential race.
Tehran radio on Sunday said high-school students would hold an annual march to the former U.S. embassy in the centre of the city on November 3 to mark the 17th anniversary of the seizure.
Across Iran students would begin the schoolday by chanting "Death to America" at morning assemblies, the radio added.
